hops.afterHeading: How a Trk receptor turns on
hops.title: The naked mole-rat's weaker TrkA
hops.text: In experiments, NGF makes mice, rats and people more sensitive to painful heat, and in mice that sensitization depends on TRPV1, a heat-sensing channel on pain neurons. The African naked mole-rat does not react this way. Its TRPV1 channel works, yet NGF fails to make it more sensitive to heat. In 2016 Damir Omerbašić, Gary Lewin and colleagues traced the difference to TrkA itself: one to three amino-acid substitutions in its kinase domain, the part that phosphorylates its partner, are enough to make the receptor hypofunctional. The animals do fine with the weaker receptor, and the authors suggest it may have been selected for.

sources.citation: Omerbašić D, Smith ESJ, Moroni M, et al. Hypofunctional TrkA accounts for the absence of pain sensitization in the African naked mole-rat. Cell Reports 17(3):748-758 (2016), PMID 27732851.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A pink, wrinkly naked mole-rat moving through an earthen tunnel beside a tuber.
image.caption: A few changes weaken naked mole-rat TrkA, helping explain why NGF fails to raise their heat-pain sensitivity.

hops.title: Finding your fingertips with your eyes closed
hops.text: Stretch your arms out to the sides, close your eyes, and slowly bring your index fingertips together in front of you. Muscle spindles, small stretch sensors inside muscles, are a major source of that sense of limb position, with help from skin and joint receptors. In 1994 mice lacking NT-3 moved their limbs abnormally, with no group Ia projections carrying limb spindle signals to spinal motor neurons and no muscle spindles in their limbs. Mice without the kinase-containing forms of TrkC also lacked those group Ia projections. And mice with one working copy of the NT-3 gene had about half the usual number of limb spindles.

sources.citation: Ernfors P, Lee KF, Kucera J, Jaenisch R. Lack of neurotrophin-3 leads to deficiencies in the peripheral nervous system and loss of limb proprioceptive afferents. Cell 77(4):503-512 (1994), PMID 7514502.

Klein R, Silos-Santiago I, Smeyne RJ, et al. Disruption of the neurotrophin-3 receptor gene trkC eliminates Ia muscle afferents and results in abnormal movements. Nature 368(6468):249-251 (1994), PMID 8145824.
Proske U, Gandevia SC. The proprioceptive senses: their roles in signaling body shape, body position and movement, and muscle force. Physiological Reviews 92(4):1651-1697 (2012), PMID 23073629.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A seated student with eyes closed bringing two index fingertips together in front of their face.
image.caption: Muscle spindles help you find your fingertips with eyes closed; mice lacking NT-3 have none in their limbs.

hops.title: The BDNF pro-domain is not throwaway packing
hops.text: It is tempting to treat a pro-domain as packing, discarded before the protein goes to work. Val66Met, a common human variant, changes one amino acid in the BDNF pro-domain. In a 2003 study, neurons making the Met form released less BDNF when stimulated, though background release was unchanged. In 2005 Zhe-Yu Chen and colleagues found a likely reason: inside neurons, sortilin, the same protein that helps p75 read uncut NGF, binds the BDNF precursor near position 66 and routes it for release on stimulation. The Met allele made up about 20 percent of alleles in a Croatian sample and 46 percent in a Korean one.

sources.citation: Egan MF, Kojima M, Callicott JH, et al. The BDNF val66met polymorphism affects activity-dependent secretion of BDNF and human memory and hippocampal function. Cell 112(2):257-269 (2003), PMID 12553913.

Chen ZY, Ieraci A, Teng H, et al. Sortilin controls intracellular sorting of brain-derived neurotrophic factor to the regulated secretory pathway. Journal of Neuroscience 25(26):6156-6166 (2005), PMID 15987945.

Pivac N, Kim B, Nedić G, et al. Ethnic differences in brain-derived neurotrophic factor Val66Met polymorphism in Croatian and Korean healthy participants. Croatian Medical Journal 50(1):43-48 (2009), PMID 19260143.

image.caption: The BDNF pro-domain is not throwaway packing: sortilin grips it to steer BDNF into regulated release.

audio.title: Trk receptors after birth: sore volunteers, a calm mole-rat and a cancer pill
audio.transcript:
The lesson so far has been about embryos, where a neuron lives or dies by the factor it can read. But these receptors do not retire at birth. Here are three stories in which grown animals, and grown people, show that Track A and its relatives are still at work.

First, a safety trial. In nineteen ninety-four, a team at Johns Hopkins tested single doses of human nerve growth factor, N G F, in healthy volunteers. The researchers saw no life-threatening reactions. But at the higher doses, volunteers reported mild to moderate muscle pain, mainly in the muscles used for chewing, speaking and swallowing, and in the trunk. Those who had it injected under the skin found the injection site tender for as long as seven weeks. Some pain-sensing neurons keep Track A into adulthood, and N G F can make them more sensitive. So if adding N G F makes pain signals stronger, what happens when an antibody mops it up? Two antibodies that neutralize N G F were later developed for animals, frunevetmab for cats and bedinvetmab for dogs, and in placebo-controlled trials they helped, modestly, with the pain of arthritis.

Second, an animal that shrugs off N G F. In experiments, N G F makes mice, rats and people more sensitive to painful heat, and in mice that depends on T R P V one, a heat-sensing channel on pain neurons. The African naked mole-rat does not react this way. Its T R P V one channel works, yet N G F does not make it more sensitive to heat. In twenty sixteen, Gary Lewin and his colleagues traced the difference to Track A itself. Between one and three amino-acid changes in its kinase domain, the part that phosphorylates its partner, are enough to weaken the receptor. The mole-rats do fine with it, and the authors suggest the change may even have been selected for.

Third, what happens when you block these kinases in people on purpose. The first Track gene was found in a human colon tumour, fused to another gene so that the kinase stayed on. Some cancers carry Track fusions like that, and a drug called larotrectinib was built to block them. A twenty eighteen report combined three trials: fifty-five patients, from four months to seventy-six years old, with seventeen different kinds of Track-fusion cancer. Independent reviewers found that the tumours shrank substantially or disappeared in seventy-five percent of them. Then a twenty twenty study looked back at ninety-six patients treated with Track inhibitors. Fifty-three percent gained weight and forty-one percent felt dizzy during treatment, and about a third of those who paused or stopped treatment had withdrawal pain. The authors linked all three effects to normal Track signalling, which helps regulate appetite, balance and pain sensitivity.

Track receptors help some developing neurons survive. After birth, they are still at work in pain, balance and appetite.
